screens.body:
A heuristic is a rule of thumb — not a law, but a principle that usually leads to good design. Usability heuristics are a checklist of ten such principles you can hold up against ANY interface and ask: "does this pass?"

Think of them like a health inspection for apps. You don't need users in the room to spot that the "delete everything" button has no confirmation — the checklist catches it.

options: Rules of thumb for judging whether an interface is usable
Strict laws that can never be broken
A type of user interview
check.question: A usability heuristic is…

screens.heading: Rules of thumb for good UX
screens.keyPoint: A health inspection checklist for interfaces.

screens.body:
Heuristic 1: always show what's happening. Loading spinners, progress bars, "message sent" confirmations — the system should never leave you staring at a frozen screen wondering if your tap registered.

Heuristic 2: speak the user's language. "Delete draft" beats "Purge ephemeral entity." Use real-world words and concepts, in the user's vocabulary — not the database's.

options: Show system status; use the user's real-world language
Hide everything to look clean
Use technical terms to sound smart
check.question: The first two heuristics:

screens.heading: Show status, speak human
screens.keyPoint: Never leave users guessing what just happened.

screens.body:
Heuristic 3: give users control and freedom — especially an emergency exit. Every destructive or committed action needs an undo, a cancel, a "back." People explore fearlessly when they know they can't break anything.

Heuristic 4: prevent errors instead of just reporting them. Grey out the "submit" button until the form is valid; confirm before deleting. A good error message is a design failure you admitted — better to make the error impossible.

options: Undo/cancel everywhere; design so errors can't happen
Let users figure out their mistakes
Error messages are enough
check.question: Control and error prevention:

screens.heading: Let them undo; stop errors early
screens.keyPoint: The best error message is one never needed.

screens.body:
Heuristic 5: be consistent. The same word should mean the same thing on every screen ("book" shouldn't sometimes mean "cancel"). Buttons that look alike should act alike. Follow platform conventions — users bring habits from every other app.

Heuristic 6: don't make people memorize. Show options instead of demanding recall — a dropdown beats "type the exact code from memory." Recognition is easy; recall is work. Good design does the remembering.

options: Same words/actions behave the same; show options instead of demanding memory
Surprise users with creative new patterns on each screen
Make users memorize codes
check.question: Consistency and memory:

screens.heading: Be consistent, do the remembering

screens.body:
Heuristic 7: flexible for everyone — shortcuts for experts, guidance for beginners. A search bar AND browsable categories. Keyboard shortcuts that don't punish mouse users.

Heuristic 8: keep it clean and minimal. Every extra element competes for attention. If it doesn't help the user's current goal, it's decoration at best and a distraction at worst. White space is a feature.

options: Serve beginners and experts; remove everything that doesn't help the goal
Add features to impress
Fill every pixel
check.question: Flexibility and minimalism:

screens.heading: Flexible yet minimal
screens.keyPoint: Shortcuts for pros, guidance for newbies, clutter for nobody.

screens.body:
Heuristic 9: when errors DO happen, help users recover. Say what went wrong in plain language and exactly how to fix it: "that card number looks short — cards have 16 digits" beats "invalid input."

Heuristic 10: help and documentation exist — but needing them is a smell. The best help is built into the interface (hints, examples, onboarding); a manual is the backup plan, not the plan.

options: Plain-language fixes for errors; built-in help over manuals
Blame the user in error messages
Hide the help pages
check.question: Error recovery and help:

screens.heading: Help them recover
screens.keyPoint: Explain the fix, not just the failure.

screens.body:
Heuristic evaluation is how you USE the list: gather 3–5 reviewers, have each judge the interface against all ten heuristics independently, then combine findings and rate each violation's severity — cosmetic, minor, major, or catastrophic.

It's cheap, fast, and needs zero users — which makes it perfect BEFORE user testing. It won't catch everything (only real users reveal real confusion), but it clears the obvious faults so testing time is spent on the interesting problems.

options: 3–5 reviewers judge the UI against heuristics, then rate severity
Asking users to memorize the heuristics
Only the designer reviews their own work
check.question: A heuristic evaluation is…

screens.heading: Judging a design with the list
screens.keyPoint: Cheap expert review before expensive user testing.

screens.body: Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — Jakob Nielsen's original 10 heuristics, in his own words; the canonical source. W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (w3.org/WAI) — official accessibility standards that overlap heavily with heuristics. Material Design guidelines (material.io) — Google's official component standards.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Read Nielsen's own 10 heuristics at NNG.
